newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamist PM to meet Israeli minister.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamist PM to meet Israeli minister.

text.p: Turkish Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, a persistent critic of Turkey's ties with Israel, is to meet the Israeli foreign minister when he visits Ankara this week, Erbakan's office said on Monday.

The Israeli embassy in Ankara had previously expressed frustration at the lack of response to its requests for a meeting between Erbakan and Foreign Minister David Levy during his two-day trip beginning on Tuesday.
"Yes, it is true, they will meet tomorrow evening," a spokesman for Erbakan told Reuters.

Israel's Ambassador Zvi Elpeleg had told Reuters earlier that Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, appeared to be trying to avoid Levy on his visit aimed at strengthening ties sought by Turkey's secularist generals.
"We have it from different channels that (Erbakan) is trying to slip away from such a meeting," Elpeleg said.

Officials at the prime minister's office, who earlier had no comment on prospects for a meeting, said the doubts might have been linked to the belief that Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party disapproved of ties with Israel.
"I think the speculation that the two leaders would not meet came from the idea that the Welfare wing (of the coalition) is not warm towards Israel," the spokesman said.
"But being leader of a political party and the prime minister of Turkey are different things. This is a state responsibility," he said.

Israel had quickly distanced itself from the ambassador's comments, saying it was up to Turkey to decide on the itinerary of a visit which comes at a time of growing defence, commercial and political ties between the two nations.
"The Turkish Foreign Ministry is the host and responsible for preparing the itinerary for the visit. Minister Levy will be glad if a meeting with Erbakan takes place but it depends on the hosts."

Erbakan won a slim plurality in general elections in 1995 after a campaign that included promises to renounce a training pact, signed by the army's number two, with Israel. He became prime minister, in coalition with conservatives, in June 1996.
Under the military deal, Israeli jets train over the Anatolian heartland, minutes from Israel's longtime rival Syria. Israel is also upgrading Turkey's ageing F-4 jets.
The military accords angered Iran, most of the Arab world and some Islamists in Turkey but the deals remain in effect despite Welfare's public opposition.

Turkey's powerful armed forces, keen to expand cooperation with Israel, have been engaged in a war of words with Erbakan, charging him with overseeing the creeping Islamisation of life in the officially secular republic.

"Ties between the two countries grew out of enhanced military cooperation but they are now poised to take on a life of their own," said a Western diplomat who monitors Turkey's policies toward the Middle East.
"A setback on the political front will not please the army," said the diplomat.
On February 28, army commanders ordered Erbakan to crack down on Islamist activism -- his core constituents. He reluctantly agreed but there has been no sign of anti-Islamist measures.
Levy is also to meet President Suleyman Demirel, Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller and other ministers from her secularist wing of the coalition. He later travels to Istanbul to meet Jewish leaders.
